items.note: The āmalaka crowns a Nāgara temple above the truncated śikhara body, with finial and vase; cogged ring-stone shape.
Earliest known crowning āmalaka of a structural temple, in fragments at Nāgari, Chitor, belongs to the fifth century A.D.
The superstructure leads the eye upward by stages, each śṛṅga being a station on the slope towards the summit.
The āmalaka is placed above the vedi of the śikhara like the third perforated stone on the Vedic altar; the central pillar offers passage to the highest region.
The superstructure shines with gavākṣas around the revolving āmalaka; its indentations sum up the buttresses of the building.
As ring-stone the āmalaka is a symbol of passage to heaven; as crown it gathers the slopes of the śikhara into unity.
Footnote locates an āmalaka carved above the railing of a casket on a structural pillar at Besnagar (P. Brown).
refs: P. Brown, Indian Architecture, Pl. IX, Fig. 4

items.note: The temple as symbol of manifestation begins from the Bindu, situated above the āmalaka.
Names of the āmalaka (Amala-śilā, Amala-sāra) describe the celestial world, of which it is symbol and Mukti-dvāra.
The stūpikā above the āmalaka is often gold; the golden kalaśa is likened to the sun on the god's dwelling.
Purāṇic account of the āmalaka tree where Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva dwell, as the image behind the āmalaka crown.
The Brahmasthāna in the garbhagṛha is pierced by the vertical shaft of the finial above the dome or āmalaka.
The temple is to be seen by circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa) and entered to be born from its dark womb; it is the seat and house of God.
Parts of the temple likened to the body of man: door as mouth, āmalaka or dome as head, image in garbhagṛha as life.
At completion the Sthapati and Sthāpaka ascend the Vimāna and perform the opening of the eyes of the Prāsāda; the Sthāpaka installs the Seed.
The Yajamāna presents the Sthāpaka and Sthapati with gold, clothes and ornaments; the merit of the work passes to the Yajamāna.
At consecration the golden Prāsāda-puruṣa is installed in the golden jar above the garbhagṛha.
The temple's central pillar rises from the Vāstupuruṣa in the Brahmasthāna to support the Prāsāda Puruṣa in the golden jar.
Kandariya temple, Khajuraho: 102' 3" long, 66' 10" wide, 101' 9" high.
The Kandariya temple stands on a high platform; four small corner shrines made it a pañcāyatana temple but no longer exist.
Kandariya temple is a Sāndhāra Prāsāda with ambulatory extended into the mahāmaṇḍapa; prāsāda and mahāmaṇḍapa contracted as one building with maṇḍapa and ardhamaṇḍapa attached.
The śukanāsā is the last halting point; maṇḍapas may not exceed its height, and the mūlamañjari carries its uromañjaris and śṛṅgas to the finial.
Terrace (jagatipītha) height is half the Prāsāda width per Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra LVI.
The Lion as devourer (grāsa) is shown with whole face, per Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra LVII (Khajuraho example).
Socle and wall mouldings of a Khajuraho Nirandhāra Prāsāda; entablature of mekhalā and antarapatra from which the śikhara curves to the āmalaka.
Khajuraho vedikā: widely projecting kumuda torus moulding on every buttress and recess.
Triple belt of images with iconography determined by direction; Viṣṇu aspects on the main bhadras (Khajuraho).
Gods in sports in the top belt, aṣṭadikpālas on the highest offset, and a śārdūla kṛtrimagrāsa in the innermost recess (Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra LVII).
Śikhara compactness from uromañjaris, karṇaśṛṅgas and naṣṭaśṛṅgas arranged in rows (Khajuraho).
The mūlamañjari is a Latārekha of the Saptaratha variety with seven facets on each side.
Corrugated āmalakas with kalaśas and bījasvaras are the dominant horizontal theme; gavākṣa jāla covers the offsets.
Citragupta Temple, Khajuraho: parts of the door surround and door height twice its width.
River goddesses and Nāgas on the doorway frame and dvārapālas on the flanking pilasters (Khajuraho).
Eight-armed Sūrya on the Duladeo (Śiva) temple embodying Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva; such an image supports meditation on Sādāśiva.
